evals.prompt: I run marketing at Fenlow, a data-pipeline observability platform (~$40k ACV, sales-led). Leadership approved one flagship event investment for next year. Our CRO keeps talking about the 14 strategic accounts we need to crack, but my team wants maximum visibility in the ecosystem - honestly a big expo-style event with partners exhibiting sounds the most exciting. We have about 3,000 people on our newsletter and we've never run an event. What should we run?
evals.expected_output: An interview-driven shape brief that surfaces the volume-versus-named-accounts conflict before ranking anything, refuses to pick the expo on visibility alone, presents 2-3 candidate shapes with one recommendation and flip conditions, and routes goals, funding and internal structure to sibling decisions without inventing any figures.
expectations: Establishes whether the goal is volume of qualified conversations or penetration of the 14-account list before ranking or recommending any shape, by asking the question or explicitly surfacing the conflict between the CRO and the marketing team
States that reach and account depth order the event shapes in exactly opposite ways, so the choice between those two axes decides the ranking
Does not recommend the expo or floor-primary shape on the strength of visibility or reach alone
States that the floor-primary shape is top of reach but bottom of account depth, so neither efficiency ordering ever selects it
Names the floor-primary promotion condition as the combination of having no audience that will travel and the ecosystem rather than the product being the year's story

Ties the shape candidates to the chosen axis: dinner or roundtable and executive summit lead if the named-account axis wins, roadshow or single-city conference lead if volume wins, rather than one generic pick
Asks for evidence that an audience would travel (customer base, mailable list, past registrations) rather than impressions before proposing a single-city conference
Presents 2-3 candidate shapes with trade-offs and exactly one recommendation
Names, for each choice made, the interview answer that would flip it next year
Routes goal mix, funding ownership and success measurement to a separate corporate event strategy decision rather than fixing goals or KPIs itself
Contains no invented headcount, city count, agenda length, ticket price or budget figure
Offers the deliverable for validation section by section rather than delivering one final block

evals.prompt: I'm head of growth at Corvassa, a compliance-automation SaaS. Budget is tight so we're planning a series of intimate invite-only dinners in Chicago and Austin next quarter - low cost, low risk, no venue contracts to sign. We don't have specific accounts picked out; the idea is to fill about ten seats per city with whatever fintech ops leaders we can pull from LinkedIn outreach and see what pipeline shakes out. Sound like a plan?
evals.expected_output: A response that removes the dinner from the menu because no named account list exists, corrects the low-risk framing by naming hospitality compliance as the dinner's top exposure, and redirects the volume goal to a shape that serves it.
expectations: Advises against the dinner series because no named account list exists
States that without named invitees the dinner degrades into a generic mixer that buys neither reach nor account depth
Removes the dinner from the menu entirely rather than keeping it as a low-ranked or fallback option
Rejects the framing that the dinners are low risk because they are small and involve no venue contracts
Places the dinner or roundtable at the top of the compliance ordering among event shapes
Names the guest's own employer's gift, hospitality or anti-bribery policy as where hosted hospitality for a named guest lands
States that an accepted invitation cannot be quietly withdrawn
Recommends a shape matched to a volume goal, such as a multi-city roadshow or single-city conference, instead of the dinners
Asks what evidence exists that an audience would travel, or what audience assets exist, before choosing between the volume shapes
Names the condition that would bring the dinner back onto the menu: a real named account list
Adds no invented headcount, seat count, budget or price figures of its own

evals.prompt: Ops lead at Merrow, a CI/CD platform. We've committed to a roadshow: my draft plan has 12 cities across the US and Europe, and each city gets a custom agenda built around local case studies and region-specific integrations, since audiences differ. Two asks: sanity-check whether 12 cities is the right number, and help me design each city's agenda - how many talks and which formats. Also, leadership hopes this becomes our flagship annual thing.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to bless a city count and installs a per-city stop rule instead, warns that bespoke per-city content destroys the roadshow's reuse economics, routes agenda design to the format-selection sibling, and redirects the annual-flagship ambition to the single-city conference shape.
expectations: Declines to validate 12 cities or to supply any specific right number of cities
Prescribes fixing a per-city stop rule before the first city: what a stop must return for the next one to run
States that the stop rule set in advance is the only defence, because the marginal-city question has no general answer
Routes the per-city economics and payback question to the goals-and-budget decision rather than guessing a count
Warns that bespoke per-city content forfeits the roadshow's core advantage
Names the reuse structure: later stops reuse one deck, one crew and one run-of-show while the first stop absorbs the setup
Distinguishes a roadshow (one program re-run across places) from a conference series (different programs across time)
Declines to design per-city agendas, talk counts or session formats, and routes internal program structure to the format-selection sibling
States that a roadshow does not become an owned annual property: it has stops, not editions
Identifies the single-city user conference as the only shape that becomes an owned annual property, and ties the flagship ambition to it
Notes that the compounding-annual-property answer can promote the single-city conference past the roadshow even though the roadshow leads reach per unit effort
Flags the per-jurisdiction registration-data and marketing-consent review triggered by stops across the US and Europe

evals.prompt: CEO of Trellick here - we make an open-source feature-flag platform, adoption is bottom-up: engineers adopt the free tier, then teams convert. A board member pointed at how well a competitor's Executive Innovation Summit works, and honestly AWS re:Invent proves big vendor events print money. I want a VP-and-above summit in Lisbon in May where we'll also publicly announce our v2 platform. My question is mostly about guest list mechanics - or would an executive roundtable be simpler?
evals.expected_output: A response that challenges the summit for a developer-led product because the seniority gate excludes the actual adopters, refuses to import the competitor's or AWS's shape without their constraints, flags that a summit cannot carry a public launch, distinguishes summit from roundtable by list assembly, and offers a developer-compatible alternative.
expectations: Warns that a seniority-gated guest list excludes the engineers who actually drive adoption under a bottom-up, developer-led motion
Identifies that inverted buying hierarchy as the main reason executive summits underperform when copied to developer products
Challenges copying the competitor's or AWS's shape: their audience, launch cadence and installed base do not transfer, so import the reasoning rather than the format
States that a summit cannot carry a public launch, so the v2 announcement needs a different shape or channel
States that a summit cannot serve an audience that evaluates products hands-on
Distinguishes a summit from a roundtable by how the list is built - assembled through nomination or application versus invitees personally known to the company - not by seniority or size
Notes that a summit needs runway that a roundtable does not
Names the summit's live risk as compliance from hosted hospitality, not budget
Establishes who the intended attendee is, or whether the goal is named-account depth versus volume, before endorsing any shape
Does not use any named company's attendance or scale figures to size the proposal
Offers at least one alternative shape consistent with a developer audience and the fixed launch, with its trade-off stated
Routes why the event is run, who funds it and how it is measured to a separate strategy decision rather than fixing them here

evals.prompt: I'm the events lead at Quenholt, a B2B data-catalog vendor. We're running our first-ever user conference in Denver this fall, and it's explicitly a one-year experiment - if it doesn't produce pipeline we won't repeat it. To make it credible with data engineers I want a fully open CFP. One wrinkle: our CPO and three VPs have each already claimed keynotes, and I can't realistically push back on them. Also, how should we later tell whether the program approach worked?
evals.expected_output: A response that talks the user out of the open CFP because both promotion conditions fail, recommends the mixed practitioner program with labelled company slots, sets the company-slot drift count as the measurement gate, and routes claim entitlement and session formatting to the sibling decisions.
expectations: Advises against the fully open CFP for this edition
Names both promotion conditions for open submissions: a compounding annual property and the political capital to tell an executive their slot did not make the program
States the collapse failure: without that political capital the open posture becomes a company-supplied program with extra administration, the worst outcome on the menu
Recommends the mixed practitioner program with labelled company slots as the default posture
Requires the company slots to be labelled as company content rather than dressed as neutral sessions
States the credibility ordering across postures: open submissions above mixed labelled above customer-story above company-supplied
Notes that open submissions also tops the effort ordering, citing the review cycle and the cost of refusing internal speakers
Does not justify a posture on cheapest-first or message-control-per-effort grounds
Sets the measurement gate as counting company slots on the final program against the planned number, watching for drift
Routes what the chosen posture entitles the event to claim about itself to the positioning decision rather than declaring the event neutral or community-run
Routes session formats and track structure to the format-selection sibling rather than designing the agenda

evals.prompt: Marketing director at Ostrave Logistics Tech. Our annual customer day has always been our own people walking through the roadmap - customers love it. This year the CEO wants to open registration to prospects and rebrand it 'FreightStack Forum - the independent gathering for supply-chain developers'. We do have a customer advisory board that meets quarterly, if that helps. Can you help me plan the agenda mix?
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes the all-internal program once prospects are marketed to, shows the independence claim fails against the single-vendor-content threshold owned by the positioning sibling, concludes the program or the marketing must change, and promotes the customer-story program on the strength of the existing advisory board.
expectations: Flags that marketing the event to people who are not customers yet changes what the program may honestly consist of
Deletes the all-internal, company-supplied program from the menu for this edition rather than merely ranking it low
States that a company-supplied program remains legitimate for the customers-only roadmap day it used to be
States that the 'independent gathering' claim is forfeit when single-vendor content dominates, citing the roughly 30-40% single-vendor-content share threshold
Attributes that threshold to the positioning sibling and labels it a reasoned default, not an industry standard
Concludes that either the program or the prospect-facing marketing must change - the two cannot both stay as-is
Recommends the customer-story program and explicitly promotes it because the customer advisory board already meets
Warns of the customer-story program's hidden cost: reference approval and legal sign-off per customer
Offers the mixed practitioner program with labelled company slots as another compliant candidate
Does not invent an alternative neutrality threshold or re-derive the positioning analysis instead of citing it
Routes final agenda mechanics such as session formats and track structure to the format-selection sibling

evals.prompt: Halvern Robotics - we sell a fleet-orchestration SDK. This year the leadership story is entirely about our partner ecosystem: 30+ integration partners, and we want the market to see them building on us. Problem: we have no event audience of our own - no past event, tiny newsletter, and customers spread worldwide who told us outright they won't fly for us. So: do we build our own partner expo, or take a large stand at RoboLogistics Expo, the industry show with about 20k attendees? If the stand: give me booth layout and staffing recommendations. And how would we judge success either way?
evals.expected_output: A floor-shape decision that works the tension between ecosystem visibility and the missing audience, presents own-floor versus third-party stand with one recommendation, refuses booth layout advice for exhibiting on someone else's floor while stating why support ends there, routes own-floor physical questions to the floor-operations sibling, and sets returning exhibitors as the own-floor success gate.
expectations: Recognizes that both floor-primary promotion conditions hold - no audience that will travel and the ecosystem as the year's story - so the floor-primary family is legitimately in play
States the floor-shape trade-off: an own floor buys ecosystem visibility while only the third-party rung borrows an audience someone else assembled
Notes that an own floor fills its own room and borrows no attendees, which the company's missing audience makes the central risk
Presents the own showcase floor and the third-party stand as candidates with trade-offs and makes exactly one recommendation

When discussing the own-floor options, names the own showcase floor as the cheapest buy of partner visibility or the program-plus-floor promotion condition as the ecosystem being what is sold this year
Declines to give booth layout and staffing recommendations for exhibiting at the third-party show
States the reason for declining: the floor-operations sibling serves the organizer who owns the hall, not a company exhibiting on someone else's floor, so support ends at naming the shape
States that limit explicitly instead of improvising generic booth tips
For an own floor, routes layout, tier specs, setup windows, staffing and traffic to the floor-operations sibling instead of answering them inline
Sets the own-floor success gate as exhibitors who return, not attendee walk-past traffic
States that attendee traffic reads on the floor's operation, which is the floor-operations sibling's outcome, not on the shape choice
Adds no invented attendee counts, exhibitor counts or booth prices of its own

evals.prompt: I'm one of the volunteer organizers of PolyglotPy, a community-run Python conference in Porto - nonprofit, about 15 volunteers, no company behind us. We're rethinking our corporate event format for next year: should we become a roadshow across three Iberian cities, or go upmarket with an executive summit for engineering leaders? Sponsors also keep asking us for more.
evals.expected_output: A response that identifies the organizer as community-run, routes the shape question to the community-pole format skill instead of applying the company-run ladder, declines to recommend the summit or roadshow from this catalog, and keeps sponsor appetite out of the shape decision.
expectations: Identifies the event as community-run, not company-run
Routes the shape question to the community-pole format-selection skill instead of answering from the company-run catalog
Stops rather than applying the company-run shape ladder: delivers no roadshow-versus-summit recommendation from this catalog
Does not recommend the executive summit for the community conference
Uses the pole names company-run and community-run while addressing what the user called corporate, mirroring the meaning rather than the label
Explains why the routing happens: the shape ladder here serves companies choosing a company-run event
Does not let sponsor appetite drive the shape choice, noting sponsor offerings are priced and delivered against a chosen shape rather than being a reason to pick one
